theory.intro: Two rectangular prisms can have the same volume even though their lengths, widths and heights are different. What matters is that the product length $\times$ width $\times$ height is the same.
facts: Different dimensions can give the **same product**, so the same volume.
Rearranging the same three dimensions (e.g. $2 \times 3 \times 4$) gives the same volume.
steps: Work out each prism's volume by multiplying its three dimensions.
Compare the products to decide if the volumes are equal.
To match a volume, find three numbers whose product equals it.

workedExamples.solution_text:
Multiply the number of cubes in one layer by the number of layers.

Prism A has $8\times3=24$ cubes in each layer and $2$ layers.
$\begin{aligned}24\times2&=48\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

Prism B has $4\times3=12$ cubes in each layer and $4$ layers.
$\begin{aligned}12\times4&=48\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

Both volumes are $48\text{ cm}^3$, although the dimensions are different.

workedExamples.question_text: A student says, “Rectangular prisms with equal volumes must have the same height.” Compare a prism with length $3$ cm, width $4$ cm and height $5$ cm with one having length $5$ cm, width $6$ cm and height $2$ cm. Is the student correct?
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}3\times4\times5&=60\text{ cm}^3\\5\times6\times2&=60\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

The student is incorrect. The volumes are equal, but the heights are $5$ cm and $2$ cm.

Changing the order of the same three dimensions also preserves volume because multiplication can be done in any order.

workedExamples.question_text: Give two rectangular prisms with different whole-number dimensions and volume $40\text{ cm}^3$. Changing only the order of the dimensions does not count as a different prism.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Choose two dimensions, then divide the volume by their product to find the third.

For length $2$ cm and width $4$ cm:
$\begin{aligned}40\div(2\times4)&=40\div8\\&=5\end{aligned}$

For length $1$ cm and width $5$ cm:
$\begin{aligned}40\div(1\times5)&=40\div5\\&=8\end{aligned}$

Sample dimensions are $2$ cm by $4$ cm by $5$ cm and $1$ cm by $5$ cm by $8$ cm.

Check:
$\begin{aligned}2\times4\times5&=40\\1\times5\times8&=40\end{aligned}$

workedExamples.question_text: List all whole-number dimension triples for rectangular prisms with volume $18\text{ cm}^3$. Count rearrangements of the same three dimensions only once.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Write each triple from smallest to largest.

With smallest dimension $1$ cm, the other two dimensions must multiply to $18$:
$1\times1\times18$, $1\times2\times9$, $1\times3\times6$.

With smallest dimension $2$ cm, the other two dimensions must multiply to $9$:
$2\times3\times3$.

A smallest dimension of $3$ cm or more would give a volume of at least $3\times3\times3=27\text{ cm}^3$, so there are no more triples.

The four dimension triples, in centimetres, are $(1,1,18)$, $(1,2,9)$, $(1,3,6)$ and $(2,3,3)$.

workedExamples.question_text: Prism A has length $3$ cm, width $4$ cm and height $7$ cm. Prism B has length $2$ cm and width $6$ cm. Find the height of prism B so that the volumes are equal.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Find prism A's volume:
$\begin{aligned}3\times4\times7&=12\times7\\&=84\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

Prism B has $2\times6=12$ cubes in one layer. Find the number of layers:
$\begin{aligned}84\div12&=7\end{aligned}$

Prism B's height is $7$ cm.

Check: $2\times6\times7=84\text{ cm}^3$.

workedExamples.question_text: A rectangular prism of modelling material has length $4$ m, width $3$ m and height $5$ m. It is reshaped into a rectangular prism with length $5$ m and width $6$ m, keeping the same volume. Find its new height.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Find the original volume:
$\begin{aligned}4\times3\times5&=12\times5\\&=60\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$

The new prism has $5\times6=30$ cubic-metre blocks in each $1$ m-high layer.
$\begin{aligned}60\div30&=2\end{aligned}$

The new height is $2$ m.

Check: $5\times6\times2=60\text{ m}^3$.

foundation.question_text:
Compare prisms $2\times3\times4$ cm and $1\times4\times6$ cm.
Do they have the same volume?
foundation.solution_text:
$2\times3\times4=24\text{ cm}^3$
$1\times4\times6=24\text{ cm}^3$
Yes, their volumes are equal.

foundation.question_text:
Compare prisms $3\times3\times5$ cm and $5\times3\times3$ cm.
What do you notice?
foundation.solution_text: Both products are $45\text{ cm}^3$. They are the same dimensions in a different order, so the volume is unchanged.

foundation.question_text: Find a whole-number set of dimensions for a prism with volume $20\text{ cm}^3$.
foundation.solution_text: One answer is $1$ cm by $4$ cm by $5$ cm because $1\times4\times5=20$.

foundation.question_text: Do prisms $2\times5\times6$ m and $3\times4\times5$ m have equal volumes?
foundation.solution_text:
$2\times5\times6=60\text{ m}^3$
$3\times4\times5=60\text{ m}^3$
Yes, the volumes are equal.

foundation.question_text:
A prism has volume $36\text{ cm}^3$ and dimensions $3\times3\times4$ cm.
Give a different dimension triple.
foundation.solution_text: $2\times3\times6=36$, so $2$ cm by $3$ cm by $6$ cm is one answer.

foundation.question_text: Explain why $2\times7\times3$ and $7\times3\times2$ describe equal volumes.
foundation.solution_text: Multiplication can be done in any order, so both products equal $42$.

development.question_text:
Prism A is $2\times4\times8$ cm.
Prism B is $4\times4\times4$ cm.
Compare their volumes and shapes.
development.solution_text:
A: $2\times4\times8=64\text{ cm}^3$
B: $4\times4\times4=64\text{ cm}^3$
They have equal volume but different dimensions.

development.question_text: Which has greater volume: $1\times6\times12$ cm or $3\times4\times6$ cm?
development.solution_text: Both products equal $72\text{ cm}^3$, so neither is greater.

development.question_text: Find two different whole-number rectangular prisms with volume $48\text{ cm}^3$.

A student says equal-volume prisms must have the same height.
Give a counterexample.
development.solution_text: $2\times3\times8$ and $3\times4\times4$ both have volume $48$, but their heights can be $8$ and $4$.

development.question_text:
A $5\times2\times9$ m prism is reshaped to length $6$ m and width $3$ m without changing volume.
Find its height.

mastery.question_text: List all unordered whole-number dimension triples for volume $24\text{ cm}^3$.

Prism P has dimensions $a\times3\times4$ and prism Q has dimensions $2\times6\times5$.
Find $a$ for equal volumes.

Can a $2\times2\times9$ prism and a $3\times3\times4$ prism have the same volume?
Explain without changing their orientation.
mastery.solution_text: $2\times2\times9=36$ and $3\times3\times4=36$. Orientation is irrelevant; the products are equal.
